title: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause
moduleName: Medical Physiology, Research Methods and Skills
source: LS5024 Female Reproductive Physiology 8oct25 no answers.pdf

cards.explanation: The lecture describes establishment before birth and a continuing decline rather than routine replenishment with new oocytes in adult life.
cards.text: The pool of available ovarian follicles is the {{c1::ovarian reserve}}.
cards.question: The pool of available ovarian follicles is the {{c1::ovarian reserve}}.

cards.explanation: Many follicles are recruited or lost while usually only one oocyte is ovulated in a natural cycle. The slide’s fixed percentages and monthly numbers are simplified estimates, not universal counts.
cards.text: Most ovarian follicles are lost through {{c1::atresia}}, rather than ovulation.
cards.question: Most ovarian follicles are lost through {{c1::atresia}}, rather than ovulation.

cards.explanation: The diagram places the first meiotic arrest before birth and before later follicular development.
cards.text: Primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and arrest in {{c1::prophase I}}.
cards.question: Primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and arrest in {{c1::prophase I}}.

cards.explanation: Each chromosome contains two sister chromatids, so chromosome number is not the same as chromatid number. The diagram’s oogonium row depends on replication stage; do not apply two chromatids to every cell-cycle stage.
cards.text: A replicated primary oocyte has {{c1::46 chromosomes}} before meiosis I.
cards.question: A replicated primary oocyte has {{c1::46 chromosomes}} before meiosis I.

cards.explanation: It is haploid, but each chromosome still has two sister chromatids.
cards.text: Meiosis I produces a secondary oocyte with {{c1::23 chromosomes}}.
cards.question: Meiosis I produces a secondary oocyte with {{c1::23 chromosomes}}.

cards.explanation: It has completed meiosis I but not meiosis II.
cards.text: An ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in {{c1::metaphase II}}.
cards.question: An ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in {{c1::metaphase II}}.

cards.explanation: This separates ovulation of the secondary oocyte from completion of the second meiotic division.
cards.text: Meiosis II in the secondary oocyte is normally completed only after {{c1::fertilisation}}.
cards.question: Meiosis II in the secondary oocyte is normally completed only after {{c1::fertilisation}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram then shows a diploid zygote following contribution from the sperm; do not label that zygote itself as haploid.
cards.text: After meiosis II, the female haploid product has 23 chromosomes with {{c1::one chromatid per chromosome}}.
cards.question: After meiosis II, the female haploid product has 23 chromosomes with {{c1::one chromatid per chromosome}}.

cards.explanation: The smaller products are polar bodies, rather than four equally resourced functional eggs.
cards.text: Oogenesis uses {{c1::asymmetric cell division}} to retain most cytoplasm in one cell.
cards.question: Oogenesis uses {{c1::asymmetric cell division}} to retain most cytoplasm in one cell.

cards.explanation: It is not genetically empty simply because it has little cytoplasm.
cards.text: A polar body contains a {{c1::haploid chromosome set}}.
cards.question: A polar body contains a {{c1::haploid chromosome set}}.

cards.explanation: The slide illustrates approximately 99% versus 1% as a teaching comparison, not an exact invariant division ratio.
cards.text: Most oocyte cytoplasm and organelles remain in the {{c1::egg lineage}} rather than the polar body.
cards.question: Most oocyte cytoplasm and organelles remain in the {{c1::egg lineage}} rather than the polar body.

cards.explanation: Dividing resources equally into four gametes would not serve the same function as sperm production.
cards.text: Retaining cytoplasm in one oocyte preserves resources for {{c1::early embryonic development}}.
cards.question: Retaining cytoplasm in one oocyte preserves resources for {{c1::early embryonic development}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture names preimplantation genetic diagnosis. Polar-body analysis informs the maternal meiotic contribution; it is not a complete test of the embryo’s paternal or later changes.
cards.text: Polar bodies can be analysed during some IVF-related {{c1::genetic testing}} procedures.
cards.question: Polar bodies can be analysed during some IVF-related {{c1::genetic testing}} procedures.

cards.explanation: Its thickness and glandular state change across the menstrual cycle.
cards.text: The inner lining of the uterus is the {{c1::endometrium}}.
cards.question: The inner lining of the uterus is the {{c1::endometrium}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the endometrial lining that undergoes cyclical shedding.
cards.text: The muscular wall of the uterus is the {{c1::myometrium}}.
cards.question: The muscular wall of the uterus is the {{c1::myometrium}}.

cards.explanation: Cervical mucus changes under ovarian hormone influence.
cards.text: The lower uterine region opening towards the vagina is the {{c1::cervix}}.
cards.question: The lower uterine region opening towards the vagina is the {{c1::cervix}}.

cards.explanation: They are associated with the funnel-shaped infundibulum and help the released oocyte enter the tube.
cards.text: Finger-like projections at the ovarian end of the uterine tube are the {{c1::fimbriae}}.
cards.question: Finger-like projections at the ovarian end of the uterine tube are the {{c1::fimbriae}}.

cards.explanation: The ampulla and isthmus are other named tube regions.
cards.text: The funnel-shaped tubal region nearest the ovary is the {{c1::infundibulum}}.
cards.question: The funnel-shaped tubal region nearest the ovary is the {{c1::infundibulum}}.

cards.explanation: The ampulla is the wider main channel in the lecture’s anatomy description.
cards.text: The narrow tubal segment between the ampulla and uterus is the {{c1::isthmus}}.
cards.question: The narrow tubal segment between the ampulla and uterus is the {{c1::isthmus}}.

cards.explanation: The slide names cilia and muscle, rather than describing the tube as a passive hollow pipe.
cards.text: Ciliated epithelium and muscular layers help {{c1::transport material along the uterine tube}}.
cards.question: Ciliated epithelium and muscular layers help {{c1::transport material along the uterine tube}}.
cards.answer: transport material along the uterine tube

cards.explanation: Cycle length is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
cards.text: Day 1 of a menstrual cycle is the onset of {{c1::menstrual bleeding}}.
cards.question: Day 1 of a menstrual cycle is the onset of {{c1::menstrual bleeding}}.

cards.explanation: Cycle timing and ovulation day vary; the day labels in the diagrams should be interpreted within that model.
cards.text: The lecture’s 28-day cycle is an {{c1::illustrative model}} rather than a fixed length for everyone.
cards.question: The lecture’s 28-day cycle is an {{c1::illustrative model}} rather than a fixed length for everyone.

cards.explanation: The diagram places follicle maturation in the first part of its model cycle.
cards.text: The ovarian phase before ovulation is the {{c1::follicular phase}}.
cards.question: The ovarian phase before ovulation is the {{c1::follicular phase}}.

cards.explanation: It is named for the corpus luteum formed from the ovulated follicle.
cards.text: The ovarian phase after ovulation is the {{c1::luteal phase}}.
cards.question: The ovarian phase after ovulation is the {{c1::luteal phase}}.

cards.explanation: The source histology labels the cavity alongside the oocyte and surrounding cells.
cards.text: The fluid-filled cavity of an antral follicle is the {{c1::antrum}}.
cards.question: The fluid-filled cavity of an antral follicle is the {{c1::antrum}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the granulosa-cell layers around it.
cards.text: The labelled coat immediately surrounding the oocyte is the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.
cards.question: The labelled coat immediately surrounding the oocyte is the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.

cards.explanation: The histology and maturation diagrams distinguish the inner granulosa compartment from the outer thecal compartment.
cards.text: The follicular cells inside the theca layer are {{c1::granulosa cells}}.
cards.question: The follicular cells inside the theca layer are {{c1::granulosa cells}}.

cards.explanation: Most other follicles in the recruited group regress instead.
cards.text: The large follicle selected to continue towards ovulation is the {{c1::dominant follicle}}.
cards.question: The large follicle selected to continue towards ovulation is the {{c1::dominant follicle}}.

cards.explanation: Granulosa and thecal cells undergo luteinisation; the corpus luteum is not the released oocyte.
cards.text: The ruptured follicle transforms into the {{c1::corpus luteum}} after ovulation.
cards.question: The ruptured follicle transforms into the {{c1::corpus luteum}} after ovulation.

cards.explanation: These secretions support luteal physiology and feedback regulation; progesterone is a major luteal product.
cards.text: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone, oestrogen and {{c1::inhibin}}.
cards.question: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone, oestrogen and {{c1::inhibin}}.

cards.explanation: Clarification: trophoblastic hCG associated with implantation maintains luteal function; fertilisation alone does not instantly produce a systemic luteal rescue signal.
cards.text: In early pregnancy, the hormone rescuing the corpus luteum is {{c1::human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG)}}.
cards.question: In early pregnancy, the hormone rescuing the corpus luteum is {{c1::human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG)}}.

cards.explanation: Luteal steroid levels then fall. The slide’s “about 10 days” refers to onset of luteal decline, not an invariant duration of every person’s luteal phase.
cards.text: Without pregnancy-related rescue, the corpus luteum {{c1::regresses}}.
cards.question: Without pregnancy-related rescue, the corpus luteum {{c1::regresses}}.

cards.explanation: They are not produced by the ovarian granulosa or thecal cells.
cards.text: FSH and LH are gonadotrophins secreted by the {{c1::anterior pituitary}}.
cards.question: FSH and LH are gonadotrophins secreted by the {{c1::anterior pituitary}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture links this to proliferation and oestrogen production.
cards.text: FSH primarily stimulates follicular {{c1::granulosa cells}}.
cards.question: FSH primarily stimulates follicular {{c1::granulosa cells}}.

cards.explanation: The androgens provide substrate for oestrogen synthesis in granulosa cells.
cards.text: LH stimulates thecal cells to produce {{c1::androgens}}.
cards.question: LH stimulates thecal cells to produce {{c1::androgens}}.

cards.explanation: This is the two-cell cooperation illustrated in the source; neither cell compartment alone describes the whole pathway.
cards.text: Thecal androgens are converted to oestrogens in {{c1::granulosa cells}}.
cards.question: Thecal androgens are converted to oestrogens in {{c1::granulosa cells}}.

cards.explanation: The slide describes relative independence up to the early antral transition; it does not mean follicles develop without local regulation.
cards.text: Early follicle growth is relatively {{c1::gonadotrophin-independent}} before later FSH/LH-dependent development.
cards.question: Early follicle growth is relatively {{c1::gonadotrophin-independent}} before later FSH/LH-dependent development.

cards.explanation: This leaves one dominant follicle in the usual natural-cycle model.
cards.text: Regression of the non-dominant developing follicles is called {{c1::atresia}}.
cards.question: Regression of the non-dominant developing follicles is called {{c1::atresia}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture names more FSH receptors and better blood supply as contributing features, not a fully settled single-factor explanation.
cards.text: Greater FSH responsiveness can help the dominant follicle survive {{c1::falling FSH levels}}.
cards.question: Greater FSH responsiveness can help the dominant follicle survive {{c1::falling FSH levels}}.

cards.explanation: This helps explain their later responsiveness to the LH surge.
cards.text: Granulosa cells of the developing dominant follicle acquire {{c1::LH receptors}}.
cards.question: Granulosa cells of the developing dominant follicle acquire {{c1::LH receptors}}.

cards.explanation: The slide presents this as part of selection. AMH has stage-dependent effects; it is not a complete explanation that one follicle simply switches off every other follicle.
cards.text: The granulosa-derived regulator named as limiting follicle recruitment is {{c1::anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)}}.
cards.question: The granulosa-derived regulator named as limiting follicle recruitment is {{c1::anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with the usual natural-cycle outcome of one dominant follicle; the aim is controlled stimulation, not an unlimited number of eggs.
cards.text: Ovarian stimulation for IVF aims to mature {{c1::multiple usable follicles}}.
cards.question: Ovarian stimulation for IVF aims to mature {{c1::multiple usable follicles}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the stimulation used to support multiple follicles; the source’s wording compresses these separate treatment goals. No regimen or dosing is supplied.
cards.text: Pituitary suppression in IVF helps prevent a premature {{c1::LH surge}}.
cards.question: Pituitary suppression in IVF helps prevent a premature {{c1::LH surge}}.

cards.explanation: The source graph also shows a smaller FSH rise; LH is the dominant ovulatory surge.
cards.text: The major pituitary peak triggering ovulation is the {{c1::LH surge}}.
cards.question: The major pituitary peak triggering ovulation is the {{c1::LH surge}}.

cards.explanation: They indicate a hormonal event associated with the fertile window rather than directly visualising oocyte release.
cards.text: Urinary ovulation predictor kits detect a surge in {{c1::LH}}.
cards.question: Urinary ovulation predictor kits detect a surge in {{c1::LH}}.

cards.explanation: This is an approximate physiological relationship; a positive kit does not prove ovulation has occurred or guarantee pregnancy.
cards.text: The lecture places the LH surge roughly {{c1::24–36 hours before ovulation}}.
cards.question: The lecture places the LH surge roughly {{c1::24–36 hours before ovulation}}.

cards.explanation: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone connects hypothalamic control with the anterior pituitary.
cards.text: The hypothalamic signal stimulating pituitary FSH and LH release is {{c1::GnRH}}.
cards.question: The hypothalamic signal stimulating pituitary FSH and LH release is {{c1::GnRH}}.

cards.explanation: This contributes to falling FSH during follicular selection. Feedback depends on context and duration, not only the hormone’s name.
cards.text: At lower or moderate follicular levels, oestrogen usually exerts {{c1::negative feedback}} on the hypothalamic–pituitary axis.
cards.question: At lower or moderate follicular levels, oestrogen usually exerts {{c1::negative feedback}} on the hypothalamic–pituitary axis.

cards.explanation: In the model, this is associated with the late follicular days around 12–14 and promotes the gonadotrophin surge.
cards.text: Sustained high preovulatory oestrogen switches the axis towards {{c1::positive feedback}}.
cards.question: Sustained high preovulatory oestrogen switches the axis towards {{c1::positive feedback}}.

cards.explanation: This helps suppress another recruitment/ovulatory cycle while the corpus luteum is active.
cards.text: High luteal progesterone contributes to {{c1::negative feedback}} on GnRH and gonadotrophin secretion.
cards.question: High luteal progesterone contributes to {{c1::negative feedback}} on GnRH and gonadotrophin secretion.

cards.explanation: This adds selective regulation of FSH alongside steroid feedback.
cards.text: Inhibin primarily suppresses pituitary {{c1::FSH}} release.
cards.question: Inhibin primarily suppresses pituitary {{c1::FSH}} release.

cards.explanation: Progesterone acts on hypothalamic thermoregulation.
cards.text: The post-ovulation rise in basal body temperature is driven by {{c1::progesterone}}.
cards.question: The post-ovulation rise in basal body temperature is driven by {{c1::progesterone}}.

cards.explanation: The curve reflects progesterone exposure; it is not an exact prospective predictor of the release time.
cards.text: Basal temperature is generally higher in the {{c1::luteal phase}} than before ovulation.
cards.question: Basal temperature is generally higher in the {{c1::luteal phase}} than before ovulation.

cards.explanation: The activity’s statement “FSH levels are promoting atresia” is clarified as reduced FSH support, not FSH being an intrinsically toxic signal.
cards.text: Non-dominant follicles undergo atresia when FSH support {{c1::falls}}.
cards.question: Non-dominant follicles undergo atresia when FSH support {{c1::falls}}.

cards.explanation: Fluid and wall changes in the mature follicle help release the secondary oocyte.
cards.text: The LH surge promotes follicular rupture and {{c1::ovulation}}.
cards.question: The LH surge promotes follicular rupture and {{c1::ovulation}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the slide: granulosa cells do not undergo oocyte meiosis. Completion produces a secondary oocyte and first polar body.
cards.text: The cell that completes meiosis I around the ovulatory signal is the {{c1::primary oocyte}}.
cards.question: The cell that completes meiosis I around the ovulatory signal is the {{c1::primary oocyte}}.

cards.explanation: They become luteal cells with a changed steroid-secretory profile.
cards.text: Transformation of granulosa and thecal cells after ovulation is {{c1::luteinisation}}.
cards.question: Transformation of granulosa and thecal cells after ovulation is {{c1::luteinisation}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s “switch” from oestrogen to progesterone should not be read as complete cessation of oestrogen secretion.
cards.text: After luteinisation, progesterone production {{c1::increases}}.
cards.question: After luteinisation, progesterone production {{c1::increases}}.

cards.explanation: Oestrogen promotes growth of the lining after menstruation.
cards.text: The endometrial rebuilding phase before ovulation is the {{c1::proliferative phase}}.
cards.question: The endometrial rebuilding phase before ovulation is the {{c1::proliferative phase}}.

cards.explanation: Progesterone changes the previously oestrogen-primed endometrium.
cards.text: The glandular phase after ovulation is the {{c1::secretory phase}}.
cards.question: The glandular phase after ovulation is the {{c1::secretory phase}}.

cards.explanation: Ovarian and uterine phase names describe different organs within the same cycle.
cards.text: The ovarian luteal phase corresponds chiefly to the uterine {{c1::secretory phase}}.
cards.question: The ovarian luteal phase corresponds chiefly to the uterine {{c1::secretory phase}}.

cards.explanation: Regression of the corpus luteum removes hormonal support for the endometrial functional layer.
cards.text: Menstruation follows withdrawal of luteal {{c1::progesterone and oestrogen}}.
cards.question: Menstruation follows withdrawal of luteal {{c1::progesterone and oestrogen}}.

cards.explanation: Vascular and inflammatory changes contribute to breakdown of the functional lining, rather than shedding the whole uterine wall.
cards.text: Constriction of endometrial vessels reduces local oxygen and {{c1::nutrient supply}}.
cards.question: Constriction of endometrial vessels reduces local oxygen and {{c1::nutrient supply}}.

cards.explanation: The source links these contractions to menstruation and the menstrual flow.
cards.text: The mediators associated with menstrual myometrial contractions are {{c1::prostaglandins}}.
cards.question: The mediators associated with menstrual myometrial contractions are {{c1::prostaglandins}}.

cards.explanation: The slide uses this as context for repair research. Its cell-culture wound-healing findings do not establish an approved treatment for skin wounds.
cards.text: Following normal menstrual shedding, the endometrium can regenerate without {{c1::scar formation}}.
cards.question: Following normal menstrual shedding, the endometrium can regenerate without {{c1::scar formation}}.

cards.explanation: This rebuilds the tissue following the menstrual shedding phase.
cards.text: Oestrogen stimulates endometrial {{c1::proliferation}}.
cards.question: Oestrogen stimulates endometrial {{c1::proliferation}}.

cards.explanation: The uterine response prepares an appropriate environment for potential implantation.
cards.text: Progesterone promotes a glandular, nutrient-rich {{c1::secretory endometrium}}.
cards.question: Progesterone promotes a glandular, nutrient-rich {{c1::secretory endometrium}}.

cards.explanation: This favours sperm passage near the fertile window; the source’s comparison is relative rather than an absolute barrier rule.
cards.text: Under oestrogen influence, cervical mucus becomes relatively {{c1::thin and watery}}.
cards.question: Under oestrogen influence, cervical mucus becomes relatively {{c1::thin and watery}}.

cards.explanation: This contributes to a barrier to sperm passage after ovulation and is used by progestogen contraception.
cards.text: Progesterone makes cervical mucus relatively {{c1::thick and less penetrable}}.
cards.question: Progesterone makes cervical mucus relatively {{c1::thick and less penetrable}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts this with oestrogen-related growth and contractility; the effect depends on physiological context.
cards.text: Progesterone tends to {{c1::reduce spontaneous myometrial contractions}}.
cards.question: Progesterone tends to {{c1::reduce spontaneous myometrial contractions}}.

cards.explanation: Progestogen is the drug class; it need not be identical to endogenous progesterone.
cards.text: The combined oral contraceptive pill contains an oestrogen and a {{c1::progestogen}}.
cards.question: The combined oral contraceptive pill contains an oestrogen and a {{c1::progestogen}}.

cards.explanation: Feedback suppresses follicular development and the ovulatory surge; it is a pre-fertilisation mechanism.
cards.text: Combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation by reducing pituitary {{c1::FSH and LH}} stimulation.
cards.question: Combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation by reducing pituitary {{c1::FSH and LH}} stimulation.

cards.explanation: This is a contraceptive mechanism distinct from ovarian suppression.
cards.text: Progestogen-mediated thickening of cervical mucus reduces {{c1::sperm passage}}.
cards.question: Progestogen-mediated thickening of cervical mucus reduces {{c1::sperm passage}}.

cards.explanation: Missed or incorrectly used pills explain some of the difference. The source’s 99.7%/91% estimates are dated, method- and time-dependent teaching figures, not universal current personalised rates.
cards.text: Perfect-use contraceptive effectiveness can exceed {{c1::typical-use effectiveness}}.
cards.question: Perfect-use contraceptive effectiveness can exceed {{c1::typical-use effectiveness}}.

cards.explanation: Oestrogen contributes to follicular suppression and cycle/endometrial stability; the comparison is not a dosing instruction.
cards.text: The progestogen component is the main {{c1::contraceptive}} component in the source’s hormone comparison.
cards.question: The progestogen component is the main {{c1::contraceptive}} component in the source’s hormone comparison.

cards.explanation: The source lists endometrial effects; these should not be promoted into a claim that routine pills terminate an implanted pregnancy or that blocking implantation is the established primary mechanism.
cards.text: Hormonal contraception can cause endometrial {{c1::thinning}}.
cards.question: Hormonal contraception can cause endometrial {{c1::thinning}}.

cards.explanation: The slide calls this the “mini pill”. Its “desogestrel 75 mg” is an apparent unit error; no dose question is made from it.
cards.text: The progestogen-only pill lacks an {{c1::oestrogen component}}.
cards.question: The progestogen-only pill lacks an {{c1::oestrogen component}}.

cards.explanation: They inhibit ovulation variably; the lecture distinguishes them from more consistently ovulation-suppressing formulations.
cards.text: Traditional progestogen-only pills act principally by thickening {{c1::cervical mucus}}.
cards.question: Traditional progestogen-only pills act principally by thickening {{c1::cervical mucus}}.

cards.explanation: This prevents assuming every progestogen-only formulation has the same degree of ovarian suppression.
cards.text: Desogestrel-containing progestogen-only pills more consistently {{c1::inhibit ovulation}}.
cards.question: Desogestrel-containing progestogen-only pills more consistently {{c1::inhibit ovulation}}.

cards.explanation: This applies to the formulations described; schedules differ for other products, so the card is not a general instruction for every progestogen-only pill.
cards.text: The traditional/desogestrel pill examples shown are taken continuously with {{c1::no hormone-free break}}.
cards.question: The traditional/desogestrel pill examples shown are taken continuously with {{c1::no hormone-free break}}.

cards.explanation: The source describes an upper-arm implant. Duration and licensing depend on product and jurisdiction, so the lecture’s three-year statement is not treated as a universal current limit.
cards.text: A contraceptive implant delivers {{c1::progestogen}} from a rod under the skin.
cards.question: A contraceptive implant delivers {{c1::progestogen}} from a rod under the skin.

cards.explanation: This assumes no alternative cause of amenorrhoea and an appropriate clinical context; hormonal contraception or treatment can obscure bleeding patterns.
cards.text: Natural menopause is identified retrospectively after {{c1::12 months without menstrual periods}}.
cards.question: Natural menopause is identified retrospectively after {{c1::12 months without menstrual periods}}.

cards.explanation: Cycles may change in interval and volume as hormone secretion becomes more variable.
cards.text: The transition before the final cessation of periods is {{c1::perimenopause}}.
cards.question: The transition before the final cessation of periods is {{c1::perimenopause}}.

cards.explanation: The transition is not a smooth monotonic fall in every oestrogen measurement.
cards.text: During perimenopause, cycle length and ovarian hormone secretion become {{c1::variable}}.
cards.question: During perimenopause, cycle length and ovarian hormone secretion become {{c1::variable}}.

cards.explanation: They illustrate a population pattern rather than a hormone threshold diagnosing every individual.
cards.text: The perimenopause graphs show gonadotrophin changes relative to the {{c1::final menstrual period}}.
cards.question: The perimenopause graphs show gonadotrophin changes relative to the {{c1::final menstrual period}}.

cards.explanation: Fewer functioning follicular cells reduce the system’s ability to generate the usual cycle, while perimenopausal levels can fluctuate.
cards.text: Declining follicle availability reduces ovarian {{c1::oestrogen secretion}} overall.
cards.question: Declining follicle availability reduces ovarian {{c1::oestrogen secretion}} overall.

cards.explanation: Not every perimenopausal cycle is anovulatory; ovulation can still occur.
cards.text: Failure to generate the usual ovulatory surge increases {{c1::anovulatory cycles}}.
cards.question: Failure to generate the usual ovulatory surge increases {{c1::anovulatory cycles}}.

cards.explanation: This is the opposite of assuming that all reproductive hormones decrease at menopause.
cards.text: Loss of ovarian steroid negative feedback raises pituitary {{c1::FSH and LH}}.
cards.question: Loss of ovarian steroid negative feedback raises pituitary {{c1::FSH and LH}}.

cards.explanation: Inhibin normally restrains FSH release; declining inhibition adds to the FSH rise.
cards.text: Reduced follicular inhibin secretion particularly increases {{c1::FSH}}.
cards.question: Reduced follicular inhibin secretion particularly increases {{c1::FSH}}.

cards.explanation: Without recurrent ovulation, the usual luteal progesterone production is lost.
cards.text: Low progesterone after menopause is consistent with the absence of regular {{c1::corpus luteum formation}}.
cards.question: Low progesterone after menopause is consistent with the absence of regular {{c1::corpus luteum formation}}.

cards.explanation: The source symptom figure also describes vasomotor and urogenital changes.
cards.text: The bone complication highlighted with low postmenopausal oestrogen is {{c1::osteoporosis}}.
cards.question: The bone complication highlighted with low postmenopausal oestrogen is {{c1::osteoporosis}}.

cards.explanation: These are symptom examples, not a requirement that every person experiences the same transition.
cards.text: Hot flushes and night sweats are {{c1::vasomotor symptoms}} associated with menopause.
cards.question: Hot flushes and night sweats are {{c1::vasomotor symptoms}} associated with menopause.

cards.explanation: The source groups these among urogenital changes; the symptoms still require appropriate clinical interpretation.
cards.text: Reduced oestrogen can contribute to vaginal {{c1::dryness and atrophy}}.
cards.question: Reduced oestrogen can contribute to vaginal {{c1::dryness and atrophy}}.

cards.explanation: The source generally describes combined replacement. Whether progestogen is needed depends particularly on whether the uterus is present.
cards.text: Hormone replacement therapy treats menopausal symptoms by replacing {{c1::oestrogen}}.
cards.question: Hormone replacement therapy treats menopausal symptoms by replacing {{c1::oestrogen}}.

cards.explanation: This clarifies why combined HRT is used; oestrogen-only regimens may be appropriate after hysterectomy. It is not a personal prescribing recommendation.
cards.text: Systemic oestrogen with an intact uterus generally requires {{c1::progestogen for endometrial protection}}.
cards.question: Systemic oestrogen with an intact uterus generally requires {{c1::progestogen for endometrial protection}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts cyclical progestogen with continuous combined use; sequential treatment can produce scheduled withdrawal bleeding.
cards.text: Sequential and continuous-combined HRT differ in the {{c1::pattern of progestogen exposure}}.
cards.question: Sequential and continuous-combined HRT differ in the {{c1::pattern of progestogen exposure}}.

cards.explanation: This is a potential benefit alongside symptom relief; the decision still depends on the individual clinical situation.
cards.text: HRT can help protect against menopausal {{c1::bone loss}}.
cards.question: HRT can help protect against menopausal {{c1::bone loss}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s combined list of cancer, stroke and clot risks must not be read as one identical risk for all HRT. Oral/transdermal and combined/oestrogen-only regimens differ.
cards.text: HRT risks depend on formulation, route, duration and {{c1::individual risk factors}}.
cards.question: HRT risks depend on formulation, route, duration and {{c1::individual risk factors}}.

cards.explanation: The source headline and preprint-style material do not establish that a new clinical immune function or treatment is settled physiology.
cards.text: The proposed immune role of postmenopausal ovaries is presented as {{c1::emerging research}}.
cards.question: The proposed immune role of postmenopausal ovaries is presented as {{c1::emerging research}}.

cards.explanation: It is an evolutionary explanation under discussion, not a conscious purpose or established single cause of menopause.
cards.text: The grandmother hypothesis proposes reproductive benefit through supporting {{c1::existing children and grandchildren}}.
cards.question: The grandmother hypothesis proposes reproductive benefit through supporting {{c1::existing children and grandchildren}}.

cards.explanation: This is a hypothesis about descendant survival, distinct from a direct physiological feedback mechanism.
cards.text: The reproductive-conflict hypothesis emphasises reduced competition for {{c1::shared resources}} between generations.
cards.question: The reproductive-conflict hypothesis emphasises reduced competition for {{c1::shared resources}} between generations.

Control of Follicular Development
•
Up until early antral phase-automatic 
development
•
After that need Follicle Stimulating Hormone 
(FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) for further 
development
•
FSH and LH known as gonadotrophins. Produced 
in anterior pituitary
•
FSH stimulates granulosa cells -proliferation and 
oestrogen production
•
LH stimulates thecal cells -proliferation and 
androgen production 
•
Androgens passed to granulosa cell 
 
use to synthesise oestrogens

• At end of first 7 days-one follicle has become DOMINANT
• Larger than the rest
• The other developing follicles degenerate - undergo ‘ATRESIA’

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 22
slides.text:
Why Does One Follicle 
Become Dominant?
• Not 100% understood
• More FSH receptors-can withstand dropping 
FSH levels
• Good blood supply
• Granulosa cells start to develop LH receptors
• Granulosa cells secrete Anti Mullerian 
Hormone – stops other follicles developing
• Just prior to ovulation, granulosa cells start 
producing progesterone

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 23
slides.text:
One dominant follicle is a problem for IVF
To maximise success in IVF need a large 
number of eggs
This means they need to prevent a 
dominant follicle forming 
Instead they want as many (within 
reason) follicles producing usable eggs
Use pituitary gland inhibitors to prevent 
a rise in LH

Ovulation Test Kits
•
An ovulation test, or an ovulation predictor kit, is 
designed to check identify the most fertile days in a 
menstrual cycle.
•
Ovulation kits work by detecting a surge in Luteinizing 
Hormone (LH) in your urine.
•
This LH surge happens 24-36 hours before the egg is 
released and so identifies when a woman is most 
fertile

slides.text:
Menstruation
• Triggered by degeneration of corpus luteum
• Drop in oestrogen and progesterone
• Constriction of uterine blood vessels- reduces 
nutrients and oxygen reaching endometrium
• Endometrium degenerates
• Myometrium contracts-caused by prostaglandins
• Endometrial arterioles then dilate
• Haemorrhage through weakened walls – 
menstrual flow (50-150ml)

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 36
slides.text:
• Every month the endometrium (lining of the uterus) rebuilds itself in 3-5 days without forming a scar 
• Researchers took the plasma part of menstrual fluid and showed it promoted migration and skin repair 
quicker than normal blood plasma
• In wounds made in human skin cells, plasma derived from menstrual fluid brought about complete repair 
in 24 hours, compared with about 40 % healing when using non-menstrual human blood plasma
• The plasma contains specific proteins that appear to enhance skin repair

Oral Contraception
•
Most common type is combined oral contraceptive pill
•
It contains a synthetic oestrogen (usually ethinylestadiol) 
and a progestogen
•
Supresses ovulation by inhibiting FSH/LH
•
Thickens cervical mucus to block sperm
•
Thins endometrium to prevent implantation
•
99.7 % effective with perfect use
•
91% effective with typical use

Oral contraceptive containing only synthetic progestogen
     (e.g. desogestrel 75mg)
•
Taken at some time each day-no break
•
Thickens cervical mucus to block sperm from entering the womb. 
•
Thins the endometrium to make it less receptive to a fertilized egg. [
•
Traditional POPs (norethisterone/levonorgestrel) primarily thicken mucus and inhibit ovulation in some cycl
•
Newer generation POPs (like desogestrel) reliably inhibit ovulation as their primary mode of action.

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 42
slides.text:
The Menopause
•
Menopause is the cessation of a woman’s 
menstrual cycle, typical age of menopause in the 
UK is 51 years. 
•
Menopause is defined as the cessation of 
periods for 1 year. 
•
Before periods come to a complete stop they 
change. Hormone levels fluctuate and there is a 
reduction in the amount of circulating oestrogen 
(produced by the tiring ovaries). 
•
Periods may become lighter, heavier, or variable 
in volume and occur at different intervals of 
time. 
•
Hormone levels fluctuate in a way that the body 
is not used to and in combination with a 
declining level of oestrogen, can cause a variety 
of symptoms.

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 44
slides.text:
Reduced follicle numbers means reduced number of 
granulosa and theca cells, so less binding sites for FSH and LH
Results in reduction of oestrogen secretion
Not enough oestrogen to trigger the LH surge so ovulation 
frequently fails to occur
So get increase in anovulatory cycles.

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 45
slides.text:
• During the menopause very low 
levels of circulating oestrogen 
actually remove negative 
feedback on the hypothalamus 
and the pituitary gland. 
• Levels of FSH and LH increase 
• The decrease in developing 
follicles also reduces the amount 
of inhibin released – causing an 
enhanced rise of FSH.

slides.text:
Hormone Replacement Therapy 
(HRT)
•
Typically replaces both oestrogen and progesterone
•
Helps with menopause symptoms
•
Helps prevent osteoporosis and muscle strength
•
Slight increase in risk of breast cancer and ovarian cancer, 
stroke and blood clots
•
Many types  - can be delivered as gel, patch, tablets
Sequential or continuous
e.g. Monthly cyclical regimen — oestrogen is taken daily and 
progestogen is given at the end of the cycle for 10–14 days, 
(monthly bleeding) or take both continuously (no bleeding)
•
regimen varies depending if peri-menopausal or post-
menopausal

slides.topic: Female Reproductive Physiology — Oogenesis, Cycle Control & Menopause — page 49
slides.text:
• Only humans and a handful of species of toothed whales are known to go through the menopause
• A study published in Nature in 2024, suggests that menopause actually allows success over the longer term.
The Grandmother Hypothesis 
having children is important for passing 
on genes to the next generation but 
ensuring their survival is important too.
 
In this case, putting effort into raising 
existing children and grandchildren might 
be a better option than continuing to 
have more offspring.
The Reproductive Conflict Hypothesis 
Wen mothers and daughters have 
children at the same time, their 
offspring compete for the same 
resources.
 If an older female instead gives up 
reproducing, then there’s less 
competition and more chance of her 
descendants surviving.
What is the evolutionary purpose of the menopause?
